hints: Look carefully at the shape of the curve at A, B, C and D. Where is the spindle growing longer, staying longest, getting shorter, and finally gone?
Remember when spindle fibres shorten to pull chromatids apart in anaphase, and when they are no longer needed and disappear in telophase. Which region shows the fibres are fully gone?
walkthrough:
**Read what the graph is really showing**

Think of the curve as the life story of the spindle. Rising means fibres are growing and reaching out. Falling means they are shortening as they pull. Flat at zero means they are gone.

Region A is rising, B is the peak, C is falling fast, D is back to zero.

**Match each region to mitosis**

In prophase the spindle forms and grows, so that is A. In metaphase chromosomes line up and fibres are at full length, so that is B. In anaphase centromeres divide and fibres shorten to pull sister chromatids to opposite poles, so that is C.

**Spot when detachment is complete**

Centromeres stay attached through metaphase and most of anaphase while pulling happens. Only after the chromatids have arrived at the poles in telophase do the spindle fibres break down and all centromeres lose their attachment. That is when mean length reaches zero, which is region D.

options.A: Region A shows fibres growing longer during prophase, when centromeres are just attaching, not detaching.
options.B: Region B is the peak length at metaphase, when all centromeres are firmly attached to the spindle at the equator.
options.C: Region C shows fibres shortening in anaphase, when centromeres have divided but are still being pulled and are still attached.
options.D: Region D shows mean length at zero in late telophase, when pulling is finished and the spindle has disassembled so all centromeres have detached.
